lessons.title: Statistics I: chi-squared and Spearman's rank correlation
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Biology — Practical assessment; handling data and statistics (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State null hypotheses and choose between chi-squared and Spearman's tests.
Calculate χ² and rs and compare with critical values.
Draw valid conclusions and state the limitations.
reviewNotes: Critical values are standard but must be checked against the GCE Board's statistical tables; one- or two-tailed Spearman use may differ.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Chi-squared
blocks.md: χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E, where O = observed and E = expected frequency. **Degrees of freedom** = number of classes − 1. Compare χ² with the critical value at **p = 0.05**: if χ² is **less** than the critical value, the difference between observed and expected is **not significant** (chance explains it). Use frequencies, not percentages, with an adequate sample (expected values ≥ 5).

blocks.title: Spearman's rank
blocks.md: rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ n(n² − 1), where d is the difference between the ranks of each pair and n is the number of pairs. rs ranges from −1 (perfect negative) through 0 (none) to +1 (perfect positive). If |rs| is **at least** the critical value for n, the correlation is significant. Rank each variable separately; for ties, use the mean of the ranks.

blocks.caption: Critical values of chi-squared at p = 0.05 for 1 to 4 degrees of freedom.
blocks.alt: A table with degrees of freedom 1 to 4 and critical values 3.84, 5.99, 7.81 and 9.49.

blocks.title: What a test can and cannot show
blocks.md: State the **null hypothesis** first, calculate the statistic, compare with the critical value (p = 0.05), then conclude in words about the biology. 'Not significant' does **not** prove that the ratio is exactly 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, only that the results are consistent with it. A significant Spearman correlation does **not** show that one variable causes the other. Use χ² only for counts in categories, not for measurements such as height.

blocks.title: Critical values used here
blocks.md: Chi-squared at p = 0.05: df 1 = 3.84; df 2 = 5.99; df 3 = 7.81; df 4 = 9.49. Spearman two-tailed at p = 0.05: n = 8, 0.738; n = 10, 0.648. These are standard table values, but check the table printed in the examination booklet used with your syllabus.

blocks.title: Worked example — chi-squared for a dihybrid cross
blocks.statement: A dihybrid cross produces 1000 offspring: 560, 170, 190 and 80 in the four classes. Test the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.
steps: df = 3; critical value 7.81. Since 6.58 < 7.81 the difference is not significant.

blocks.title: Worked example — Spearman's rank
blocks.statement: At 10 sites, rainfall rank (1–10) and plant height rank are: heights 2,1,4,3,6,5,8,10,7,9 against ranks 1–10. Calculate rs. (Σd² = 16.)
steps: rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ n(n² − 1) with n = 10, so n(n² − 1) = 990.
rs = 0.90 > 0.648, so the positive correlation is significant.

lessons.title: Statistics II: standard deviation and the t-test
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Biology — Practical assessment; handling data and statistics (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of a sample.
Compare two means with the t-test and state the conclusion.
Evaluate experimental design: sample size, controls, reliability.
reviewNotes: Critical t values (df 8, 10, 12, 14, 18) are standard table values; df = 14 value 2.14 (two-tailed, 5 %) is used in the problem.
Welch's version of the t-test (different formulae for degrees of freedom) is not covered; check which version is expected.
Yield and leaf data are invented.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Standard deviation
blocks.md: Mean x̄ = Σx ÷ n. Sample standard deviation s = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)]. A **small** s means data are clustered around the mean (precise); a **large** s means they are spread out. About 95 % of values lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean if data are normally distributed. Error bars on graphs often show ± 1 SD.

blocks.title: Unpaired t-test
blocks.md: t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ÷ √(s₁²÷n₁ + s₂²÷n₂); degrees of freedom = n₁ + n₂ − 2. Null hypothesis: **no significant difference** between the two means. If |t| is **greater** than the critical value at p = 0.05 for those degrees of freedom, reject the null hypothesis. Two-tailed critical values at p = 0.05: df 8 = 2.31; df 10 = 2.23; df 12 = 2.18; df 18 = 2.10.

blocks.caption: Mean leaf lengths of sun and shade leaves (n = 6 each).
blocks.alt: A bar chart with two bars: sun leaves 24.5 mm and shade leaves 30.0 mm.

blocks.title: Choose the right test
blocks.md: **t-test**: two means of continuous data. **Chi-squared**: frequencies in categories. **Spearman**: correlation between two ranked variables. Many students use the t-test on counts or chi-squared on measurements. Calculate to enough decimal places, state the null hypothesis and the degrees of freedom, and conclude in words about the biology. Statistics cannot rescue a poor design: use random samples, a sufficient sample size, and control variables.

blocks.title: Evaluating an investigation
blocks.md: Improve **reliability** with repeats and larger samples; improve **validity** by controlling variables (e.g. leaf age, same plant species, same time of day); reduce bias by random sampling. Anomalous results should be identified, checked and, if justified, excluded with explanation. Identify limitations (e.g. few sites, one season) and suggest improvements.

blocks.title: Worked example — mean and SD
blocks.statement: Leaf lengths (mm) in sun: 22, 25, 24, 27, 23, 26. Calculate the mean and the standard deviation.

blocks.title: Worked example — t-test
blocks.statement: Shade leaves (mm): 29, 31, 28, 33, 30, 29 give mean 30.0 and s = 1.79. Test the difference from sun leaves (mean 24.5, s = 1.87), n = 6 each.
steps: 5.20 > 2.23: the difference is significant; reject the null hypothesis.
